claim: GLT1-SEP was designed by introducing SEP into the second intracellular loop of GLT1a, between two proline residues (P199 and P200).
source: First, we designed the GLT1-SEP probe for FRAP measurements by introducing SEP into the second intracellular loop of GLT1a, between two proline residues (P199 and P200).
evidence: This is a direct methodological description of the construct design.

claim: GLT1a accounts for 90% of total GLT1 expression in astrocytes in the rat brain.
source: GLT1a was selected because it accounts for 90% of total GLT1 expression in astrocytes in the rat brain, with GLT1b and GLT1c accounting for ~6% and ~1%, respectively (Holmseth et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holmseth et al., 2009.

claim: GLT1b accounts for approximately 6% of total GLT1 expression in astrocytes in the rat brain.
source: GLT1a was selected because it accounts for 90% of total GLT1 expression in astrocytes in the rat brain, with GLT1b and GLT1c accounting for ~6% and ~1%, respectively (Holmseth et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holmseth et al., 2009.

claim: GLT1c accounts for approximately 1% of total GLT1 expression in astrocytes in the rat brain.
source: GLT1a was selected because it accounts for 90% of total GLT1 expression in astrocytes in the rat brain, with GLT1b and GLT1c accounting for ~6% and ~1%, respectively (Holmseth et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holmseth et al., 2009.

claim: The GLT1-SEP construct was cloned under the gfaABC1D promoter for astrocyte-specific expression.
source: Next, aiming at astrocyte-specific expression, we cloned the construct under the gfaABC1D promoter (Lee et al., 2008; Figure 1A; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: GLT1-SEP produces a current response to glutamate application similar to wild-type GLT1.
source: Functional probing of GLT1-SEP expressed in HEK cells shows a prominent current response to glutamate application, similar to that wild-type GLT1 (WT); top diagram, theta-glass pressure pipette application; traces, one-cell examples (Vh = −70 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The normalized current-voltage dependencies of GLT1 and GLT1-SEP are indistinguishable.
source: Summary of tests shown in (A): normalised current-voltage dependencies of GLT1 (mean ± SEM; n = 8) and GLT1-SEP (n = 4) are indistinguishable; current values normalised at Vh = −70 mV (absolute values 194 ± 29 pA and 81 ± 10 pA for GLT1 and GLT1-SEP, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The absolute current in GLT1-SEP expressing cells was on average approximately 50% lower than wild-type GLT1.
source: However, the absolute current in GLT1-SEP expressing cells was on average ~50% lower (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), possibly because of the lower expression compared to native GLT1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transient acidification to pH 5.5 suppresses cell-surface GLT1-SEP fluorescence.
source: Transient acidification (~10 s pH 5.5 puff, upper row) supresses cell-surface GLT1-SEP fluorescence whereas transient membrane NH4+ permeation (~10 s NH4Cl puff, lower row) reveals the cytosolic fraction of GLT1-SEP; one-cell example.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Transient membrane NH4+ permeation reveals the cytosolic fraction of GLT1-SEP.
source: Transient acidification (~10 s pH 5.5 puff, upper row) supresses cell-surface GLT1-SEP fluorescence whereas transient membrane NH4+ permeation (~10 s NH4Cl puff, lower row) reveals the cytosolic fraction of GLT1-SEP; one-cell example.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The average cell-surface fraction R of GLT1-SEP in astroglial processes is 0.72 ± 0.18 (n = 8 cells).
source: Average cell-surface fraction R of GLT1-SEP (summary of experiments shown in D and E); dots, individual cells (connecting lines indicate the same cell); grey bars, average values (R mean ± SEM: 0.51 ± 0.15, n = 6 for somata; 0.72 ± 0.18, n = 8 for processes; soma boundaries in two cells were poorly defined).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Between 2/3 and 3/4 of all cellular GLT1-SEP were exposed to the extracellular space in astroglial processes.
source: Systematic quantification of these experiments (Figure 1E) provided an estimate of the average GLT1-SEP surface fraction in astroglial processes, R = 0.72 ± 0.18 (n = 8 cells, Figure 1F). In other words, between 2/3 and 3/4 of all cellular GLT1-SEP were exposed to the extracellular space.
evidence: This claim is derived from the experimental data and represents an interpretation of the R value.

claim: GLT1-SEP expression in HEK cells was significantly lower than wild-type GLT1 expression.
source: To understand further the relationship between the expression levels of native GLT1 and GLT1-SEP in HEK cells, we firstly compared immunostaining in cells expressing GLT1 or GLT1-SEP, and found that GLT1-SEP staining was indeed significantly lower (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: In HEK cells, GLT1 expression was twice as high as that of GLT1-SEP based on western blot analysis.
source: Secondly, we compared expression of GLT1 variants in HEK cells using quantitative western blot (normalised against α-tubulin; n = 6 samples per condition). In these samples, GLT1 expression was twice as high as that of GLT1-SEP, and genetic deletion of the intracellular C-terminus (GLT1ΔC-SEP variant) did not change this difference significantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Genetic deletion of the intracellular C-terminus (GLT1ΔC-SEP variant) did not significantly change the expression difference between GLT1 and GLT1-SEP in HEK cells.
source: Secondly, we compared expression of GLT1 variants in HEK cells using quantitative western blot (normalised against α-tubulin; n = 6 samples per condition). In these samples, GLT1 expression was twice as high as that of GLT1-SEP, and genetic deletion of the intracellular C-terminus (GLT1ΔC-SEP variant) did not change this difference significantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The decrease in the surface expression of GLT1-SEP and in its transporter current in HEK cells were matched, suggesting that adding the extracellular SEP tag had no detectable effect on glutamate uptake properties of GLT1.
source: Thus, the decrease in the surface expression of GLT1-SEP and in its transporter current in HEK cells (compared with the case of wild-type GLT1) were matched, suggesting that adding the extracellular SEP tag had no detectable effect on glutamate uptake properties of GLT1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the matching of expression and current data.

claim: GLT1-SEP was almost exclusively expressed in astrocytes in mixed cultures of neurons and glial cells due to the gfaABC1D promoter.
source: We next expressed GLT1-SEP in mixed cultures of neurons and glial cells. Thanks to the gfaABC1D promoter, the probe was almost exclusively expressed in astrocytes.
evidence: This claim is based on the known specificity of the gfaABC1D promoter.

claim: Brief acidification of the extracellular medium to pH 5.5 reversibly suppressed GLT1-SEP fluorescence.
source: Firstly, we confirmed that the observed fluorescence comes mainly from the membrane fraction of GLT-SEP. Indeed, brief acidification of the extracellular medium to pH 5.5 (10 s pipette puff with pH-adjusted bath medium) reversibly suppressed GLT1-SEP fluorescence (Figure 1D, upper row).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Proton permeation of the cell membrane with NH4Cl could reveal both intra- and extracellular GLT1-SEP fractions in a reversible fashion.
source: Conversely, proton permeation of the cell membrane (10 s puff with NH4Cl) could reveal both intra- and extracellular GLT1-SEP fractions, in a reversible fashion (Figure 1D, lower row).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The characteristic lifetime of the membrane GLT1-SEP fraction is approximately 22 seconds.
source: These estimates suggest that the characteristic lifetime of the membrane GLT1-SEP fraction, as given by (k1)−1, is ~22 s.
evidence: This claim is derived from kinetic analysis of FRAP data.

claim: The best-fit estimate for GLT1-SEP membrane turnover gave k1 = 0.045 ± 0.003 s−1, k-1 = 0.020 ± 0.001 s−1, and Cin = 0.30 ± 0.01.
source: The best-fit estimate gave (Figure 2B): k1 = 0.045 ± 0.003 s−1, k-1 = 0.020 ± 0.001 s−1, and Cin = 0.30 ± 0.01.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The value of Cin (intracellular fraction of GLT1-SEP) obtained from FRAP experiments was indistinguishable from the value of 1−R obtained using the proton permeation method.
source: Reassuringly, the value of Cin (intracellular fraction of GLT1-SEP) obtained in these experiments was indistinguishable from the value of 1−R = 0.28 obtained using a fully independent proton permeation method (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim compares results from two independent methods.

claim: Deleting the C-terminus had only a moderate effect on the intracellular fraction of transporters (Cin = 0.35 ± 0.01).
source: FRAP experiments in the GLT1ΔC-SEP expressing cells (Figure 2C) showed that deleting the C-terminus had only a moderate effect on the intracellular fraction of transporters (Cin = 0.35 ± 0.01) but reduced the GLT1 membrane lifetime by nearly a half (to ~14 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deleting the C-terminus reduced the GLT1 membrane lifetime by nearly a half (to approximately 14 seconds).
source: FRAP experiments in the GLT1ΔC-SEP expressing cells (Figure 2C) showed that deleting the C-terminus had only a moderate effect on the intracellular fraction of transporters (Cin = 0.35 ± 0.01) but reduced the GLT1 membrane lifetime by nearly a half (to ~14 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The C-terminus could play an important role in retaining GLT1 in the plasma membrane.
source: This finding suggests that the C-terminus could play an important role in retaining GLT1 in the plasma membrane, even though a steady-state membrane-intracellular compartment ratio remains almost unaffected.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the FRAP data on GLT1ΔC-SEP.

claim: The membrane GLT1-SEP does not necessarily predict the intracellular GLT1-SEP pattern.
source: Intriguingly, this comparison revealed that the membrane GLT1-SEP does not necessarily predict the intracellular GLT1-SEP pattern: the latter could display prominent clustering features (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The intracellular GLT1-SEP could display prominent clustering features.
source: Intriguingly, this comparison revealed that the membrane GLT1-SEP does not necessarily predict the intracellular GLT1-SEP pattern: the latter could display prominent clustering features (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At least in some cases the membrane dynamics of GLT1 could be specific to microscopic regions of the cell.
source: Thus, at least in some cases the membrane dynamics of GLT1 could be specific to microscopic regions of the cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the heterogeneous distribution patterns observed.

claim: The pattern of wild-type GLT1 with respect to PSD95 clusters deviates from the evenly random distribution towards closer spatial association.
source: Indeed, the classical nearest-neighbour analysis indicated that the pattern of wild-type GLT1 and GLT1-SEP with respect to PSD95 clusters deviates from the evenly random distribution towards closer spatial association (Figure 3C), and that these transporter molecules also tend to form short-distance (up to 50 nm) clusters among themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMLM analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GLT1-SEP with respect to PSD95 clusters deviates from the evenly random distribution towards closer spatial association.
source: Indeed, the classical nearest-neighbour analysis indicated that the pattern of wild-type GLT1 and GLT1-SEP with respect to PSD95 clusters deviates from the evenly random distribution towards closer spatial association (Figure 3C), and that these transporter molecules also tend to form short-distance (up to 50 nm) clusters among themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMLM analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild-type GLT1 and GLT1-SEP transporter molecules tend to form short-distance (up to 50 nm) clusters among themselves.
source: Indeed, the classical nearest-neighbour analysis indicated that the pattern of wild-type GLT1 and GLT1-SEP with respect to PSD95 clusters deviates from the evenly random distribution towards closer spatial association (Figure 3C), and that these transporter molecules also tend to form short-distance (up to 50 nm) clusters among themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMLM analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GLT1ΔC-SEP showed spatial dissociation (distancing) with PSD95 clusters.
source: In contrast, the species with deleted C-terminus, GLT1ΔC-SEP, showed spatial dissociation (distancing) with PSD95 clusters (Figure 3B,C) while displaying dense molecular clustering among themselves, to the extent that the latter is not distinguishable from uniform packing at a high local density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; this analysis does not cover higher-order, longer-distance GLT1ΔC-SEP clustering, which is evident in Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMLM analysis shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: GLT1ΔC-SEP displays dense molecular clustering among themselves, to the extent that the latter is not distinguishable from uniform packing at a high local density.
source: In contrast, the species with deleted C-terminus, GLT1ΔC-SEP, showed spatial dissociation (distancing) with PSD95 clusters (Figure 3B,C) while displaying dense molecular clustering among themselves, to the extent that the latter is not distinguishable from uniform packing at a high local density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; this analysis does not cover higher-order, longer-distance GLT1ΔC-SEP clustering, which is evident in Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SMLM analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The C-terminus of GLT1 plays a critical role in its cellular membrane turnover and in the surface (and submembrane) expression pattern of the protein.
source: These observations indicate that the C-terminus of GLT1 plays a critical role not only in its cellular membrane turnover but also in the surface (and submembrane) expression pattern of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SMLM and FRAP data on GLT1ΔC-SEP.

claim: In baseline conditions, the best-fit values for GLT1-SEP lateral mobility were Cmob = 0.76 ± 0.01 and mobile-fraction diffusivity D = 0.152 µm2/s.
source: In baseline conditions, the best-fit values were Cmob = 0.76 ± 0.01 and mobile-fraction diffusivity D = 0.152 µm2/s (diffusion time τD = 1.75 ± 0.03 s, Materials and methods), thus giving the average diffusivity (accounting for mobile and immobile molecules) D* = Cmob·D = 0.114 µm2/s (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The average diffusivity of GLT1-SEP (accounting for mobile and immobile molecules) in baseline conditions is D* = 0.114 µm2/s.
source: In baseline conditions, the best-fit values were Cmob = 0.76 ± 0.01 and mobile-fraction diffusivity D = 0.152 µm2/s (diffusion time τD = 1.75 ± 0.03 s, Materials and methods), thus giving the average diffusivity (accounting for mobile and immobile molecules) D* = Cmob·D = 0.114 µm2/s (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This claim is derived from FRAP data analysis.

claim: The average lateral diffusivity of GLT1-SEP appears in correspondence with the average lateral diffusivity of GLT1 measured earlier with QDs.
source: This value appears in correspondence with the average lateral diffusivity of GLT1 measured earlier with QDs (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015), although it is higher than the values reported using a different QD approach (Al Awabdh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim compares the current results with previous studies using QDs.

claim: When glutamate was briefly applied immediately before and after the photobleaching pulse, diffusivity of the mobile-fraction only did not appear to be affected (τD = 1.73 ± 0.03 s).
source: When glutamate was briefly applied immediately before and after the photobleaching pulse, diffusivity of the mobile-fraction only did not appear to be affected (τD = 1.73 ± 0.03 s) whereas its size increased significantly (Cmob = 0.88 ± 0.003), giving average D* = 0.135 µm2/s, an increase of ~18% compared to control (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When glutamate was briefly applied, the size of the mobile fraction increased significantly (Cmob = 0.88 ± 0.003), giving average D* = 0.135 µm2/s, an increase of approximately 18% compared to control.
source: When glutamate was briefly applied immediately before and after the photobleaching pulse, diffusivity of the mobile-fraction only did not appear to be affected (τD = 1.73 ± 0.03 s) whereas its size increased significantly (Cmob = 0.88 ± 0.003), giving average D* = 0.135 µm2/s, an increase of ~18% compared to control (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Glutamatergic activity could boost overall membrane mobility of GLT1 transporters.
source: This result suggested that glutamatergic activity could boost overall membrane mobility of GLT1 transporters, a conclusion similar to that drawn earlier using QDs (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015; Al Awabdh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the FRAP data and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Deleting the C-terminus of GLT1-SEP does not alter its mobility in basal conditions (Cmob = 0.815 ± 0.003; D* = 0.117 µm2/s).
source: We next found that deleting the C-terminus of GLT1-SEP does not alter its mobility in basal conditions (Cmob = 0.815 ± 0.003; D* = 0.117 µm2/s) but appears to block the mobility-boosting effect of glutamate application (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Deleting the C-terminus of GLT1-SEP appears to block the mobility-boosting effect of glutamate application.
source: We next found that deleting the C-terminus of GLT1-SEP does not alter its mobility in basal conditions (Cmob = 0.815 ± 0.003; D* = 0.117 µm2/s) but appears to block the mobility-boosting effect of glutamate application (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of metabotropic glutamate receptors had no detectable effect on GLT1-SEP mobility in baseline conditions (Cmob = 0.795 ± 0.003; D* = 0.121 µm2/s).
source: A similar result was obtained when metabotropic glutamate receptors were blocked by a pharmacological cocktail: no detectable effect on GLT1-SEP mobility in baseline conditions (Cmob = 0.795 ± 0.003; D* = 0.121 µm2/s) but suppression of the glutamate-induced mobility increase (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of metabotropic glutamate receptors suppressed the glutamate-induced mobility increase of GLT1-SEP.
source: A similar result was obtained when metabotropic glutamate receptors were blocked by a pharmacological cocktail: no detectable effect on GLT1-SEP mobility in baseline conditions (Cmob = 0.795 ± 0.003; D* = 0.121 µm2/s) but suppression of the glutamate-induced mobility increase (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ATP application had no effect on GLT1-SEP mobility.
source: Because purinergic receptors mediate a major signalling cascade in brain astroglia (Verkhratsky and Nedergaard, 2018), we asked whether ATP application alters mobility of GLT1-SEP and detected no effect (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Cross-linking surface GLT-SEP with antibodies reduced the FRAP-measured transporter mobility fivefold.
source: Finally, to assess sensitivity and the dynamic range of our FRAP protocol we cross-linked surface GLT-SEP, by incubating cultures briefly (10 min in humidified incubator) with either IgY antibody (100 μg/ml, chicken polyclonal, Merck AC146) or with the anti-GFP antibody (100 μg/ml, chicken polyclonal, Abcam ab13970). The cross-linkage reduced the FRAP-measured transporter mobility fivefold (Figure 4H), confirming high sensitivity and general suitability of the present FRAP method.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Diffusivity of GLT1-SEP in the plasma membrane in hippocampal slices was similar, if somewhat slower, than that in cultures.
source: However, the small-ROI FRAP experiments (as in Figure 4A) in slices showed that diffusivity of GLT1-SEP in the plasma membrane was similar, if somewhat slower, than that in cultures (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Elevated excitatory activity increased GLT1-SEP mobility in hippocampal slices, which could be reversed by blocking spiking activity with TTX.
source: Elevated excitatory activity increased GLT1-SEP mobility, which could be reversed by blocking spiking activity with TTX (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A truncated sham-protein probe carrying an extracellular SEP domain showed no changes in lateral diffusion under elevated network activity.
source: We confirmed that this effect was not due to some unknown concomitants of increased network activity that might affect astrocyte membrane properties per se: a truncated sham-protein probe carrying an extracellular SEP domain showed no changes in lateral diffusion under this protocol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by control FRAP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Application of the vehicle DMSO on its own had no effect on the activity-dependent increase in GLT1-SEP diffusion.
source: Conversely, application of the vehicle DMSO on its own had no effect on the activity-dependent increase in GLT1-SEP diffusion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by control FRAP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminus suppressed the activity-dependent mobility increase of GLT1-SEP in hippocampal slices.
source: Again, deletion of the C-terminus or the pharmacological blockade of metabotropic glutamate receptors suppressed the activity-dependent mobility increase (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of metabotropic glutamate receptors suppressed the activity-dependent mobility increase of GLT1-SEP in hippocampal slices.
source: Again, deletion of the C-terminus or the pharmacological blockade of metabotropic glutamate receptors suppressed the activity-dependent mobility increase (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Buffering intracellular Ca2+ with BAPTA-AM suppressed the activity-dependent mobility increase of GLT1-SEP in hippocampal slices.
source: Because metabotropic glutamate receptors engage a major Ca2+ signalling cascade in astroglia (Porter and McCarthy, 1997), we asked if buffering intracellular Ca2+ with BAPTA-AM is involved and found this to be the case (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Blocking the calcium and calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin produced suppression of the activity-dependent mobility increase of GLT1-SEP.
source: Investigating this further, we blocked the calcium and calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin, which produced similar suppression (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Non-selective protein kinase inhibition with the antibiotic staurosporine left the excitation-induced rise of GLT1-SEP mobility intact.
source: However, non-selective protein kinase inhibition with the antibiotic staurosporine left the excitation-induced rise of GLT1-SEP mobility intact (Figure 5H), thus narrowing the range of the candidate molecular mechanisms involved.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: 70–75% of GLT1-SEP dwell on the surface of rat brain astroglia.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching-based imaging shows that 70–75% of GLT1-SEP dwell on the surface of rat brain astroglia, recycling with a lifetime of ~22 s.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: GLT1-SEP recycles with a lifetime of approximately 22 seconds.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching-based imaging shows that 70–75% of GLT1-SEP dwell on the surface of rat brain astroglia, recycling with a lifetime of ~22 s.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Genetic deletion of the C-terminus accelerates GLT1-SEP membrane turnover.
source: Genetic deletion of the C-terminus accelerates GLT1-SEP membrane turnover while disrupting its surface pattern, as revealed by single-molecule localisation microscopy.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Genetic deletion of the C-terminus disrupts GLT1-SEP surface pattern.
source: Genetic deletion of the C-terminus accelerates GLT1-SEP membrane turnover while disrupting its surface pattern, as revealed by single-molecule localisation microscopy.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by SMLM data.

claim: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP.
source: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP, involving its C-terminus, metabotropic glutamate receptors, intracellular Ca2+, and calcineurin-phosphatase activity, but not the broad-range kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The excitatory activity-induced boost in surface mobility of GLT1-SEP involves its C-terminus.
source: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP, involving its C-terminus, metabotropic glutamate receptors, intracellular Ca2+, and calcineurin-phosphatase activity, but not the broad-range kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The excitatory activity-induced boost in surface mobility of GLT1-SEP involves metabotropic glutamate receptors.
source: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP, involving its C-terminus, metabotropic glutamate receptors, intracellular Ca2+, and calcineurin-phosphatase activity, but not the broad-range kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The excitatory activity-induced boost in surface mobility of GLT1-SEP involves intracellular Ca2+.
source: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP, involving its C-terminus, metabotropic glutamate receptors, intracellular Ca2+, and calcineurin-phosphatase activity, but not the broad-range kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The excitatory activity-induced boost in surface mobility of GLT1-SEP involves calcineurin-phosphatase activity.
source: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP, involving its C-terminus, metabotropic glutamate receptors, intracellular Ca2+, and calcineurin-phosphatase activity, but not the broad-range kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The excitatory activity-induced boost in surface mobility of GLT1-SEP does not involve broad-range kinase activity.
source: Excitatory activity boosts surface mobility of GLT1-SEP, involving its C-terminus, metabotropic glutamate receptors, intracellular Ca2+, and calcineurin-phosphatase activity, but not the broad-range kinase activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Membrane turnover, rather than lateral diffusion, is the main 'redeployment' route for the immobile fraction (20–30%) of surface-expressed GLT1.
source: The results suggest that membrane turnover, rather than lateral diffusion, is the main 'redeployment' route for the immobile fraction (20–30%) of surface-expressed GLT1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing turnover and diffusion rates.

claim: Glutamate uptake by astroglial transporters confines excitatory transmission to the synaptic cleft.
source: Glutamate uptake by astroglial transporters confines excitatory transmission to the synaptic cleft.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in neuroscience.

claim: The main glial glutamate transporter GLT1 maintains extracellular glutamate at nanomolar levels.
source: The main glial glutamate transporter GLT1 (EAAT2) maintains extracellular glutamate at nanomolar levels, thus constraining its excitatory action mainly to the synaptic cleft (Moussawi et al., 2011; Zheng and Rusakov, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moussawi et al., 2011 and Zheng and Rusakov, 2015.

claim: Synaptic vesicles release approximately 3000 glutamate molecules.
source: Because synaptic vesicles release ~3000 glutamate molecules (Savtchenko et al., 2013) and because glutamate uptake cycle can take tens of milliseconds (Wadiche et al., 1995b), large numbers of transporter molecules have to be available near synapses to buffer the escaping glutamate (Lehre and Danbolt, 1998; Bergles et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Savtchenko et al., 2013.

claim: Glutamate uptake cycle can take tens of milliseconds.
source: Because synaptic vesicles release ~3000 glutamate molecules (Savtchenko et al., 2013) and because glutamate uptake cycle can take tens of milliseconds (Wadiche et al., 1995b), large numbers of transporter molecules have to be available near synapses to buffer the escaping glutamate (Lehre and Danbolt, 1998; Bergles et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wadiche et al., 1995b.

claim: Large numbers of transporter molecules have to be available near synapses to buffer the escaping glutamate.
source: Because synaptic vesicles release ~3000 glutamate molecules (Savtchenko et al., 2013) and because glutamate uptake cycle can take tens of milliseconds (Wadiche et al., 1995b), large numbers of transporter molecules have to be available near synapses to buffer the escaping glutamate (Lehre and Danbolt, 1998; Bergles et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Lehre and Danbolt, 1998 and Bergles et al., 2002.

claim: The high occurrence of GLT1 in astroglial plasma membranes ensures that regular network activity does not overwhelm glutamate transport.
source: Indeed, the high occurrence of GLT1 in astroglial plasma membranes (Danbolt, 2001) ensures that regular network activity does not overwhelm glutamate transport (Bergles and Jahr, 1998; Diamond and Jahr, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Danbolt, 2001; Bergles and Jahr, 1998; and Diamond and Jahr, 2000.

claim: Intense excitation can prompt glutamate escape from the immediate synapse, leading to activation of extrasynaptic receptors or even neighbouring synapses.
source: However, intense excitation can prompt glutamate escape from the immediate synapse, leading to activation of extrasynaptic receptors or even neighbouring synapses (Lozovaya et al., 1999; Arnth-Jensen et al., 2002; Scimemi et al., 2004; Henneberger et al., 2020; Kopach et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The reduced availability of GLT1 in the synaptic environment has long been associated with pathologic conditions such as neurodegenerative diseases, stroke, or addiction.
source: Ultimately, the reduced availability of GLT1 in the synaptic environment has long been associated with pathologic conditions such as neurodegenerative diseases, stroke, or addiction (Maragakis and Rothstein, 2004; Fontana, 2015; Kruyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maragakis and Rothstein, 2004; Fontana, 2015; and Kruyer et al., 2019.

claim: A growing body of evidence has suggested the involvement of GLT1's carboxyl-terminal domain and protein kinase C in its cellular trafficking and turnover.
source: A growing body of evidence has suggested the involvement of its carboxyl-terminal domain and protein kinase C (Kalandadze et al., 2002; González et al., 2007) and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (Underhill et al., 2015), also engaging ubiquitin-dependent processes (González et al., 2007; González-González et al., 2008; Martínez-Villarreal et al., 2012) and constitutive protein sumoylation (García-Tardón et al., 2012; Foran et al., 2014; Piniella et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Single-particle tracking with quantum dots has detected high surface mobility of GLT1 in astroglia.
source: In recent elegant studies, single-particle tracking with quantum dots (QDs) has detected high surface mobility of GLT1 in astroglia (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015; Al Awabdh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murphy-Royal et al., 2015 and Al Awabdh et al., 2016.

claim: Lateral diffusivity of GLT1 transporters was boosted by local glutamatergic activity, suggesting the use-dependent surface supply of GLT1 towards active synapses.
source: Lateral diffusivity of transporters was boosted by local glutamatergic activity, thus suggesting the use-dependent surface supply of GLT1 towards active synapses (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015; Al Awabdh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murphy-Royal et al., 2015 and Al Awabdh et al., 2016.

claim: Synthetic QDs almost certainly prevent their link-labelled molecules from the membrane-intracellular compartment turnover.
source: However, synthetic QDs almost certainly prevent their link-labelled molecules from the membrane-intracellular compartment turnover and, at the same time, do not label any newly appearing molecules on the cell surface.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of QD labeling.

claim: Synthetic QDs do not label any newly appearing molecules on the cell surface.
source: However, synthetic QDs almost certainly prevent their link-labelled molecules from the membrane-intracellular compartment turnover and, at the same time, do not label any newly appearing molecules on the cell surface.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of QD labeling.

claim: The molecule-tracking observations relying solely on QDs could miss important changes in the composition and/or mobility of the studied molecular species due to their continuous recycling in the membrane.
source: Thus, the molecule-tracking observations relying solely on QDs could miss important changes in the composition and/or mobility of the studied molecular species due to their continuous recycling in the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of QD-based tracking.

claim: GLT1 is endocytosed constitutively, in a clathrin-dependent manner, taking the transporter into rapidly recycling endosomes containing EEA1 and Rab4.
source: It has previously been shown that GLT1 is endocytosed constitutively, in a clathrin-dependent manner, taking the transporter into rapidly recycling endosomes containing EEA1 and Rab4 (Martínez-Villarreal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Martínez-Villarreal et al., 2012.

claim: The common neuronal glutamate transporter GLAST undergoes clathrin-dependent endocytosis.
source: Earlier studies have also indicated that the common neuronal glutamate transporter GLAST also undergoes clathrin-dependent endocytosis (González et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to González et al., 2007.

claim: The characteristic lateral diffusion time of the GLT1-SEP mobile fraction (approximately 1.75 s) was much shorter than its membrane lifetime of approximately 22 s.
source: Importantly, the characteristic lateral diffusion time of the GLT1-SEP mobile fraction (~1.75 s) was much shorter than its membrane lifetime of ~22 s.
evidence: This is a comparison of two measured parameters.

claim: The assessment of mobile transporter diffusivity should not be noticeably influenced by its membrane turnover.
source: This implies that the assessment of mobile transporter diffusivity, obtained here with GLT1-SEP or earlier with QDs, should not be noticeably influenced by its membrane turnover.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of diffusion time and membrane lifetime.

claim: Earlier studies found that GLT1 near synapses diffuse orders of magnitude slower than all transporters on average.
source: For instance, the earlier studies found that GLT1 near synapses diffuse orders of magnitude slower than all transporters on average (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015; Al Awabdh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murphy-Royal et al., 2015 and Al Awabdh et al., 2016.

claim: The membrane-intracellular compartment exchange, rather than lateral diffusion, could be a preferred mechanism of the transporter turnover near synapses.
source: Thus, the membrane-intracellular compartment exchange, rather than lateral diffusion, could be a preferred mechanism of the transporter turnover near synapses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of diffusion rates and turnover rates.

claim: 10,000–15,000 GLT1 molecules are present within 1 μm3 of CA1 hippocampal neuropil.
source: Indeed, it has been estimated that small excitatory synapses release ~3000 glutamate molecules per vesicle (Savtchenko et al., 2013) and that 10,000–15,000 GLT1 molecules are present within 1 μm3 of CA1 hippocampal neuropil (Lehre and Danbolt, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lehre and Danbolt, 1998.

claim: A rapid burst of several single-vesicle release events, or repeated multi-vesicular release, could lead to a relatively high occupancy, if not saturation, of immobile GLT1 within the 1 μm3 perisynaptic volume.
source: Therefore, a rapid burst of several single-vesicle release events, or repeated multi-vesicular release, could lead to a relatively high occupancy, if not saturation, of immobile GLT1 within the 1 μm3 perisynaptic volume.
evidence: This is an inference based on the number of glutamate molecules released and the number of GLT1 molecules present.

claim: The potential importance of high GLT1 diffusivity for regulating the waveform of excitatory synaptic currents was suggested earlier.
source: The potential importance of high GLT1 diffusivity for regulating the waveform of excitatory synaptic currents was suggested earlier (Murphy-Royal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murphy-Royal et al., 2015.

claim: At small central synapses in situ, the kinetics of individual AMPA currents should not depend on glutamate buffering outside the synaptic cleft.
source: At small central synapses in situ, however, the kinetics of individual AMPA currents should not depend on glutamate buffering outside the synaptic cleft (Zheng et al., 2008; Savtchenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2008 and Savtchenko et al., 2013.

claim: Intense glutamatergic activity can boost glutamate escape from the cleft.
source: Nonetheless, intense glutamatergic activity can boost glutamate escape from the cleft (Lozovaya et al., 1999), in which case lateral movement of astroglial transporters could indeed contribute to the efficiency of uptake.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lozovaya et al., 1999.

claim: In the case of intense glutamatergic activity, lateral movement of astroglial transporters could contribute to the efficiency of uptake.
source: Nonetheless, intense glutamatergic activity can boost glutamate escape from the cleft (Lozovaya et al., 1999), in which case lateral movement of astroglial transporters could indeed contribute to the efficiency of uptake.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of lateral diffusion under intense activity.

claim: Blocking kinase activity promotes glutamate uptake.
source: This is in line with previous studies which have shown that blocking kinase activity promotes glutamate uptake (Adolph et al., 2007; Li et al., 2015): lateral mobility might be one of the mechanisms assisting this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adolph et al., 2007 and Li et al., 2015.

claim: Lateral mobility might be one of the mechanisms assisting glutamate uptake when kinase activity is blocked.
source: This is in line with previous studies which have shown that blocking kinase activity promotes glutamate uptake (Adolph et al., 2007; Li et al., 2015): lateral mobility might be one of the mechanisms assisting this process.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of lateral mobility.

claim: Regulation of GLT1 by calcineurin has previously been shown on the transcriptional level.
source: Although regulation of GLT1 by calcineurin has previously been shown on the transcriptional level (Sompol et al., 2017), calcineurin is also known to directly dephosphorylate membrane proteins such as connexin-43 (Tencé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sompol et al., 2017.

claim: Calcineurin is known to directly dephosphorylate membrane proteins such as connexin-43.
source: Although regulation of GLT1 by calcineurin has previously been shown on the transcriptional level (Sompol et al., 2017), calcineurin is also known to directly dephosphorylate membrane proteins such as connexin-43 (Tencé et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tencé et al., 2012.

claim: In transfected astrocytes, the all-variant GLT1 level was higher than in non-transfected cells.
source: In the transfected astrocytes, the all-variant GLT1 level was higher than in non-transfected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In astrocytes transfected with GLT1ΔC-SEP, GLT1 level was 25–50% higher than that for GLT1 in non-transfected cells.
source: In the astrocytes transfected with the GLT1-SEP variant with the truncated cytosolic carboxy-terminal (GLT1ΔC-SEP, Materials and methods)) we were able to detect only endogenous GLT1 levels as the antibody does not recognise GLT1ΔC-SEP. In the transfected astrocytes, GLT1 level was 25–50% higher than that for GLT1 in non-transfected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The endogenous GLT1 expression was perfectly stable in non-transfected cells that are present in transfected culture samples.
source: We also confirmed that the endogenous GLT1 expression was perfectly stable in non-transfected cells that are present in transfected culture samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The membranes of both transfected and non-transfected cells are densely and relatively uniformly packed with the respective GLT1 variants.
source: These immunostaining data have simply confirmed that the membranes of both transfected and non-transfected cells are densely and relatively uniformly packed with the respective GLT1 variants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunostaining data.

claim: The fact that the population of functional astroglial glutamate transporters is effectively replaced several times per minute must be an intriguing discovery.
source: The fact that the population of functional astroglial glutamate transporters is effectively replaced several times per minute must be an intriguing discovery.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the turnover rate findings.

claim: A recent study used fixed-tissue immunocytochemistry in pure astroglial cultures to find only approximately 25% of all GLT1 expressed in the cell membrane.
source: Interestingly, a recent study used fixed-tissue immunocytochemistry in pure astroglial cultures to find only ~25% of all GLT1 expressed in the cell membrane (Underhill et al., 2015), thus relating a boost in transporter numbers to the presence of neuronal connections (in the mixed cultures slices employed here).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Underhill et al., 2015.

claim: A boost in transporter numbers is related to the presence of neuronal connections.
source: Interestingly, a recent study used fixed-tissue immunocytochemistry in pure astroglial cultures to find only ~25% of all GLT1 expressed in the cell membrane (Underhill et al., 2015), thus relating a boost in transporter numbers to the presence of neuronal connections (in the mixed cultures slices employed here).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results in pure astroglial cultures versus mixed cultures.
